title: Peeking and stopping early
reading_md:
**What it is.** Peeking means checking a fixed-horizon test again and again and stopping as soon as p < 0.05. Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so the false positive rate rises well above 5%. A 1999 paper reports that with up to five looks it rose from 5% to about 14%. There are two fixes: commit to the sample size and the duration in advance, or use a sequential method with always-valid p-values, as Optimizely adopted.

**How to work it out.**

Planned duration (days) = required n per variant / daily users per variant, rounded up to whole days, then up to whole weeks

Worked example. The test needs 7,600 users per variant and gets 1,100 users per variant a day.

- 7,600 / 1,100 = 6.909
- Round up to 7 days
- 7 days is one full week

So the test runs 7 days and is analysed once, at the end. Whole weeks matter because behaviour differs by weekday, and a partial week biases the mix.

**In the interview.** "The test was significant on day 3. Do we stop?" A good answer: no, unless a sequential method was planned. Early swings are common, and peeking inflates false positives.

**Common mistakes.**

- Stopping as soon as significance appears.
- Extending a test until it becomes significant.
- Believing peeking only matters for small tests.
- Watching nothing at all. Monitor guardrails for harm while the test runs, but make the success decision at the planned end.
